subject: History
context: Choose the correct option from the given options and complete the sentences :
stem: The earliest museum in the world was discovered in the excavations at the city of ____.
solution: Ur. The remains of the earliest known museum in the world were found during the excavations of Ur, an ancient city of Mesopotamia (present-day Iraq). The Babylonian princess Ennigaldi-Nanna had collected there a set of old objects, each carefully labelled with a description, and this collection is regarded as the first museum. Delhi, Harappa and Kolkata are not connected with the earliest museum; the first museum in India is the Indian Museum at Kolkata, founded in 1814.

subject: History
context: Choose the correct option from the given options and complete the sentences :
stem: The first Chief Minister of Maharashtra was ____.
solution: Yashwantrao Chavhan. The bilingual State of Bombay was reorganised and the State of Maharashtra came into being on 1 May 1960 after the Samyukta Maharashtra Movement, and Yashwantrao Chavhan took oath as its first Chief Minister on that day. He is remembered as the 'Shilpakar' (architect) of modern Maharashtra. Vasantrao Naik (the longest-serving Chief Minister of the state), Vasantdada Patil and Shankarrao Chavhan all held the office later.

subject: History
context: Choose the correct option from the given options and complete the sentences :
stem: The Sanskrit text of 'Hitopadesh' was translated into German by ____.
solution: Friedrich Max Muller. Max Muller was a German Orientalist and Indologist who translated the Sanskrit text 'Hitopadesh' into German, edited and translated the Rigveda, and brought out the great fifty-volume series 'The Sacred Books of the East'. His work is a landmark of Orientalist historiography. James Mill wrote 'The History of British India' and represents colonial historiography, Mountstuart Elphinstone was a British administrator who wrote a history of India, and Sir John Marshall was the Director General of the Archaeological Survey of India under whom the Harappan civilisation was discovered.

subject: History
context: Identify the wrong pair in the following and rewrite it :
stem:
Identify the wrong pair in the following set of Marathi plays and their playwrights, and rewrite it correctly:
(i) Raigadala Jevha Jag Yete — Vasant Kanetkar
(ii) Tilak ani Agarkar — Vishram Bedekar
(iii) Sashtang Namaskar — Acharya Atre
(iv) Ekach Pyala — Annasaheb Kirloskar

options.label: A
options.text: Raigadala Jevha Jag Yete — Vasant Kanetkar

solution: The wrong pair is (iv) 'Ekach Pyala' — Annasaheb Kirloskar. 'Ekach Pyala', the famous Marathi tragedy on the ruin caused by drink, was written by Ram Ganesh Gadkari. Annasaheb Kirloskar is the father of Marathi Sangeet Natak and wrote 'Sangeet Shakuntal' and 'Sangeet Saubhadra'. Rewritten correctly : Ekach Pyala — Ram Ganesh Gadkari (or, Sangeet Saubhadra — Annasaheb Kirloskar). The other three pairs are correct : 'Raigadala Jevha Jag Yete' is by Vasant Kanetkar, 'Tilak ani Agarkar' by Vishram Bedekar, and the farce 'Sashtang Namaskar' by Acharya P. K. Atre.

subject: History
context: Identify the wrong pair in the following and rewrite it :
stem:
Identify the wrong pair in the following set of thinkers and their books, and rewrite it correctly:
(i) Leopold von Ranke — The Secret of World History
(ii) Michel Foucault — Archaeology of Knowledge
(iii) Karl Marx — Das Kapital
(iv) Rene Descartes — Reason in History

options.label: A
options.text: Leopold von Ranke — The Secret of World History

solution: The wrong pair is (iv) Rene Descartes — 'Reason in History'. 'Reason in History' was written by the German philosopher George Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, who held that history moves forward through the dialectic of thesis, antithesis and synthesis. Rene Descartes, the French philosopher who insisted on doubt and verification as the test of truth, wrote 'Discourse on the Method'. Rewritten correctly : Rene Descartes — Discourse on the Method (or, Hegel — Reason in History). The other three pairs are correct : Leopold von Ranke wrote 'The Secret of World History' and insisted that history be written only from original documents, Michel Foucault wrote 'The Archaeology of Knowledge', and Karl Marx wrote 'Das Kapital'.

subject: History
context: Complete the activity as per given instructions (any two) :
stem:
Complete the following chart. As printed, the top box reads 'Libraries in India and Cities' and it branches into two columns, 'Cities' and 'Name of the Library'. Under 'Cities' four cities are already printed, and against each of them the blank in the 'Name of the Library' column has to be filled in:

| Cities | Name of the Library |
|---|---|
| Kolkata | ______ |
| Delhi | ______ |
| Hyderabad | ______ |
| Mumbai | ______ |

Write the name of the well-known library situated in each of these four cities.
solution:
The completed chart of libraries in India and their cities is:

| Cities | Name of the Library |
|---|---|
| Kolkata | The National Library of India |
| Delhi | Delhi Public Library |
| Hyderabad | State Central Library (formerly the Asafia Library) |
| Mumbai | The Library of the Asiatic Society of Mumbai |

The National Library at Belvedere, Kolkata is the largest library in India and holds the copyright deposit of every book published in the country. The Delhi Public Library, set up in 1951 with the help of UNESCO, was the first public library of its kind in India. The State Central Library at Hyderabad, founded as the Asafia Library, preserves a rich collection of Urdu, Persian and Arabic manuscripts. The Asiatic Society of Mumbai, founded in 1804, has a famous collection of rare books and manuscripts. (Other acceptable Mumbai answers are the David Sassoon Library and the Mumbai Marathi Grantha Sangrahalaya.)

subject: History
context: Write short notes on (any two) :
stem: Write a short note on : Applied History.
solution: Applied History is the branch of history that puts historical knowledge to practical use in present-day life. History is not merely a record of the past to be studied in a classroom; the information gathered by historical research can be used to solve present problems and to serve public needs, and that use is Applied History. Its main fields are : the conservation and preservation of tangible heritage such as forts, caves, temples, monuments, sculptures, coins, manuscripts and documents; the preservation of intangible heritage such as folk arts, festivals, crafts, oral traditions and languages; the running of museums, archives and libraries; the development of heritage tourism, heritage walks and guided tours; the planning of cities and villages with regard to their historic character; the making of films, serials and documentaries on historical themes; art direction, costume design and advertising; and the fields of archaeology, epigraphy, numismatics, genealogy and museology. Applied History thus creates public awareness of our heritage, helps in its protection, and provides professional and employment opportunities to students of history.

subject: History
context: Write short notes on (any two) :
stem: Write a short note on : Maratha Style of Painting.
solution: The Maratha style of painting developed in Maharashtra in the seventeenth to nineteenth centuries under the patronage of the Maratha rulers, the Peshwas and their sardars. It survives chiefly as wall paintings (murals) in the wadas, temples and mathas of Maharashtra — for example in the wadas at Menavali and Wai, at Satara, Nashik, Nagpur and Aundh and in the remains of Shaniwarwada in Pune — and also as miniature paintings and illustrated manuscripts on paper and cloth. In its treatment it blends the conventions of the Mughal and Rajput schools with the older local tradition of Chitrakathi (Paithan) painting. Its subjects are episodes from the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and the Bhagavata, the life of Shri Krishna, portraits of rulers and sardars, court scenes and processions, battles and hunting scenes, festivals and scenes of everyday life. Natural mineral and vegetable colours were used, figures were drawn with bold flowing outlines and usually shown in profile, and the compositions are crowded with lively detail. The Maratha paintings are an important source for the dress, ornaments, weapons, architecture and social customs of the Maratha period.

subject: History
subtopic: Applied History and Research in Various Fields
context: Write short notes on (any two) :
stem: Write a short note on : Sthalakosh.
solution: A Sthalakosh is a place-encyclopaedia, that is, a reference volume that brings together in one place all the available information about a particular locality, town or region. It records the geographical situation and physical features of the place, the origin and meaning of its name, its history from ancient times to the present, its rulers and the important events connected with it, its forts, temples, monuments and archaeological remains, its inscriptions, coins and old documents, its fairs, festivals, crafts, occupations and folk traditions, and the eminent persons born or associated with it. A sthalakosh is prepared by collecting oral accounts from local people, by consulting gazetteers, old records, inscriptions and family papers, and by observation in the field. It is a valuable tool of Applied History : it preserves local history that would otherwise be lost, it provides ready material to students, teachers and researchers, it helps in planning the conservation of local heritage, and it serves guides, tourists and the local administration.

subject: History
context: Explain the following statements with reasons (any two) :
stem: Foucault called his method, 'the archaeology of knowledge'.
solution: Michel Foucault, the French thinker, rejected the older way of writing history as a smooth, continuous and linear story of progress running from the past to the present. In his book 'The Archaeology of Knowledge' he argued that the historian should instead examine the ideas, beliefs, institutions and forms of speech of a particular period on their own terms, and should look for the breaks and discontinuities between one period and the next. He held that in every age there are hidden rules which decide what may be said, what counts as true and what counts as knowledge, and that these rules are bound up with power. To bring them to light the historian has to dig through the layers of documents and discourse of a period, exactly as an archaeologist digs through the layers of an excavation site and reads each stratum separately to reconstruct the life of that level. Because his method is this layer-by-layer excavation of the past of knowledge itself, Foucault called it 'the archaeology of knowledge'.

subject: History
context: Explain the following statements with reasons (any two) :
stem: Bakhar is an important type of historical documents.
solution: A bakhar is a form of narrative prose writing in Marathi which developed in the Maratha period and describes the deeds of a king or a family, or a particular event such as a battle. 'Sabhasad Bakhar' on Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj, 'Bhausahebanchi Bakhar' and 'Panipatchi Bakhar' on the third battle of Panipat, 'Chitnisanchi Bakhar' and 'Holkaranchi Kaifiyat' are well-known examples. Bakhars are important historical documents for several reasons. They were written in or close to the period they describe, often by officers, chroniclers or eyewitnesses who had personal knowledge of the events, so they preserve first-hand information. They give detailed accounts of political events, wars and the strategy of battles, of the administration, the court, the revenue system and the army, and also of the dress, food, customs, festivals and beliefs of the people, which the official state papers do not record. They preserve the form of the Marathi language and its prose style of that time. They fill many gaps left by inscriptions and state records, and provide a continuous narrative. They must however be used critically, because a bakhar is often written to praise its hero and mixes legend, miracle and exaggeration with fact, and its dates are sometimes inaccurate; the historian therefore has to verify it against other sources.

subject: History
context: Explain the following statements with reasons (any two) :
stem: Expertise in History is important in the film industry.
solution: A very large number of films, television serials and documentaries are based on historical themes and on the lives of historical personalities. To make such a film convincing, everything shown on the screen must belong to the period of the story — the costumes, ornaments, hair-styles, weapons, coins, vehicles, utensils, furniture, the architecture of the forts, wadas and palaces, the language spoken, and the customs, rituals and manners of the society of that time. Only a person who has studied history can supply this information, check the script for factual mistakes and guide the art director, the set designer and the costume designer. A historian is also needed to search archives, old newspapers, photographs, paintings and documents while making a documentary, and to advise the producer so that the film does not distort facts or hurt public sentiment. Historians therefore work in the film industry as researchers, script consultants and advisers on art direction and costume, and expertise in History is important in the film industry.

subject: History
subtopic: Applied History and Research in Various Fields
context: Explain the following statements with reasons (any two) :
stem: It is essential to study the history of technology.
solution: Technology has shaped human life in every age, from the stone tools of the earliest men to the machines and computers of today, and the study of its history is essential for several reasons. It explains how human society itself changed : the invention of agriculture, the wheel, metal-working, the printing press, the steam engine and the computer each transformed occupations, trade, transport, warfare, the economy and the social order. It helps the historian and the archaeologist to interpret and to date the objects they find, because pottery, beads, metal implements, coins and structures can be placed in time only if the techniques of making them are known. It preserves and revives traditional Indian skills and crafts which would otherwise be lost — the metallurgy of the rustless iron pillar at Delhi and of Wootz steel, ship-building, the weaving of fine textiles, the making of natural dyes, and the engineering of temples, forts and water systems. It is indispensable in conservation work, since a monument or an object can be restored correctly only if the conservator knows the original material and the original method of construction. It also warns us of the harmful effects of technology, such as pollution and the exhaustion of resources, and helps in planning future technology wisely. Finally it has opened new fields of research and careers — the history of science and medicine, industrial archaeology and museology.

He was also part of the previous Indian hockey teams in 1928 and 1932, which played at Olympics and won gold medals. 29th August, the birth date of Dhyan Chand is celebrated as National Sports Day in India. He was known as the 'Wizard of Hockey'. He was honoured with a 'Padmabhushan' in 1956.
stem: State your opinion about the game of Hockey.
solution: Hockey is an outdoor team game played by two teams of eleven players each, who use a curved stick to drive a hard ball into the opponent's goal within a fixed time. In my opinion it is one of the finest games, for the following reasons. It demands speed, stamina, quick reflexes, accurate stick-work and constant alertness, so it keeps the body fit and the mind sharp. Since a goal can be scored only by passing the ball from player to player, it teaches team spirit, co-operation, discipline and obedience to the captain and the umpire, and it develops leadership and the ability to take instant decisions. It needs only a stick, a ball and a ground, so it can be played in villages and towns alike and does not depend on costly equipment. Hockey also has a proud place in our national life : India won six successive Olympic gold medals in hockey between 1928 and 1956 under players such as Major Dhyan Chand, and this brought the country honour and international recognition. Today cricket has drawn away much of the attention and money that hockey deserves, and I feel that hockey, our traditionally strongest game, should be encouraged in schools by providing grounds, coaching and tournaments so that it regains its former glory.

subject: History
context: Answer the following questions in detail (any two) :
stem: What is feminist historiography ?
solution: Feminist historiography means the writing of history from the point of view of women, that is, the re-examination of the past with women placed at the centre of the enquiry. Traditional history was written almost entirely by men and about men — about kings, wars, treaties and politics — and women were either left out altogether or mentioned only as queens and mothers. Feminist historiography arose along with the women's movement in the twentieth century and asks a different set of questions : what work did women actually do, what was their place in the family, in agriculture, in industry and in the market, what property and legal rights did they have, what education was open to them, how were their marriage, widowhood and health governed by custom, and how did they resist the injustices done to them. It therefore studies the ordinary woman and not only the famous one, and it uses new kinds of sources — diaries, letters, autobiographies, oral accounts, folk songs, court records and household papers — because the official records say little about women. Simone de Beauvoir's 'The Second Sex' (1949), which argued that woman is always defined as the 'other' in a male-dominated society, was a landmark in this thinking. In India this approach has led to studies of the women's reform movements, of the participation of women in the freedom struggle, and of the lives of working and peasant women. Feminist historiography thus corrects the one-sided picture of the past, restores women to their rightful place in history, and gives strength to the demand for equality in the present.

subject: History
subtopic: Art, Applied Art and Professional Opportunities
context: Answer the following questions in detail (any two) :
stem: What kind of professional opportunities are available in the field of Arts ?
solution: The field of arts offers a wide range of professional opportunities, in the visual arts, in the applied or commercial arts and in the performing arts. In the visual arts a trained person may work as a painter, sculptor, potter, print-maker or illustrator, and may sell work through art galleries and exhibitions. In the applied and commercial arts there is work as a commercial artist, graphic designer, web and user-interface designer, advertising and layout artist, animator, cartoonist, photographer, film and television art director, set designer, costume and make-up designer, interior designer, textile and fashion designer, jewellery designer, and designer of toys, packaging and furniture. In the performing arts one may become a professional singer, instrumentalist, dancer, actor, choreographer, music director or sound and lighting designer, and may work in theatre, films, television and the recording industry. Teaching is another large field — art teachers in schools, lecturers in colleges of art and music, and private tutors and coaches. Those who study art history may work as art historians and critics, as curators and guides in museums and art galleries, as conservators and restorers of paintings, sculptures and manuscripts, as valuers and consultants in the art market and in auction houses, and as writers on art in newspapers and magazines. Arts and crafts also give self-employment to a great many artisans, and there are careers in art therapy, in event and exhibition management, and in the organisations of the government that promote art, such as the Akademis and the Department of Archaeology and Museums.

subject: History
context: Answer the following questions in detail (any two) :
stem: What is Powada ?
solution: A Powada is a heroic ballad in Marathi. It is a long narrative poem, composed and sung by a shahir, which describes in a vigorous and stirring style the brave deeds of a hero or an important historical event such as a battle or the capture of a fort. The shahir sings it standing, in a loud and rapid rhythm, with expressive gestures, and he is accompanied by a chorus and by instruments such as the daf, the dholki, the tuntune and the manjiri; the audience joins in the refrain. The powada is composed in simple, forceful, everyday language so that ordinary people can understand it, and its purpose is to praise the hero, to record the event and to rouse the listeners' feelings of courage and self-respect. The earliest known powada is the one composed by the shahir Agnidas on the killing of Afzal Khan by Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj in 1659; another famous one is Tulsidas's powada on Tanaji Malusare and the battle of Sinhagad. Later shahirs such as Ram Joshi, Prabhakar, Honaji Bala and Anantphandi carried on the tradition, and in modern times Shahir Amar Sheikh, Annabhau Sathe and Gavankar used the powada in the freedom struggle, in the Samyukta Maharashtra movement and for social awakening. Because powadas were composed close to the events they describe, they are also an important source of the history of Maharashtra, though they must be used carefully as they praise their hero and sometimes exaggerate.

subject: History
context: Answer the following questions in detail (any two) :
stem: Explain any three types of tourism.
solution:
Tourism is classified according to the purpose for which people travel. Three important types are :

(1) Historical or heritage tourism — People travel to see places of historical importance : forts such as Raigad, Sindhudurg and Shivneri, the rock-cut caves of Ajanta, Ellora and Elephanta, temples, stupas, palaces, memorials, and World Heritage Sites such as the Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus. Such tourism creates pride in and awareness of our heritage, and provides work for guides, and to hotels, transport and craftsmen; it also creates the need to conserve the monuments properly.

(2) Religious or pilgrimage tourism — People travel to places of worship and pilgrimage such as Pandharpur, Shirdi, Tuljapur, Nashik, Varanasi, Tirupati, Ajmer, Bodh Gaya and Amritsar, and to fairs and festivals such as the Kumbha Mela. This is the oldest and the largest kind of tourism in India; it goes on throughout the year and it supports the whole economy of the pilgrim towns.

(3) Natural or eco-tourism — People travel to enjoy natural beauty and to observe wildlife : hill stations like Mahabaleshwar and Matheran, sea beaches, waterfalls, caves, the Kaas plateau of flowers, and national parks and sanctuaries such as Tadoba, Melghat and Dajipur. Eco-tourism is planned so that the visitors do not damage the environment, and it makes local people the partners and the protectors of nature.

(Other recognised types are medical or health tourism, agro-tourism, adventure tourism, sports tourism, educational tourism and entertainment tourism.)

subject: Political Science
context: Choose the correct option from given options and complete the statements :
stem: In Maharashtra ____ seats are reserved for women in local self-governing institutions.
solution: 50%. The 73rd and 74th Amendments to the Constitution reserved not less than one-third of the seats in panchayats and municipal bodies for women. Maharashtra went further and raised this reservation to 50 per cent in its village panchayats, panchayat samitis, zilla parishads, municipal councils and municipal corporations, so that today half the seats and half the posts of chairperson in local self-governing institutions in Maharashtra are held by women. This has brought a very large number of women into public life.

subject: Political Science
subtopic: Farmers' Movement and the Green Revolution
context: Choose the correct option from given options and complete the statements :
stem: To increase agricultural production and become self-sufficient with regard to food grains ____ was initiated.
solution: Green revolution. From the middle of the 1960s India adopted the Green Revolution — high-yielding variety seeds, chemical fertilisers and pesticides, assured irrigation and mechanised farming — precisely in order to raise the output of food grains, mainly wheat and rice, and to end the country's dependence on imported grain. The White Revolution (Operation Flood) relates to milk production, the Industrial Revolution to manufacturing, and 'Water revolution' is not a recognised programme in this context.

subject: Political Science
context: State whether the following statements are true or false. Give reasons for your answers (any two) :
stem: State whether the following statement is true or false and give the reason for your answer : Under special circumstances the Election Commission holds re-elections in a particular constituency for a second time.
solution: True. Ordinarily polling in a constituency is held only once, on the day announced by the Election Commission. But the Commission is bound to secure a free and fair election, and so in special circumstances it cancels the poll and orders a fresh poll, called re-polling, either in the whole constituency or in the affected polling booths. Such circumstances are booth capturing, large-scale bogus voting or other malpractice, violence or rioting on the day of polling, the snatching, damaging or tampering of ballot boxes or of electronic voting machines, a serious technical failure of the machines, or a natural calamity that prevents voting. Again, if a contesting candidate of a recognised party dies before the poll, the election in that constituency is countermanded and held afresh. In all these situations the election in that particular constituency is held for a second time.

subject: Political Science
context: State whether the following statements are true or false. Give reasons for your answers (any two) :
stem: State whether the following statement is true or false and give the reason for your answer : Secrecy in the working of Government has increased due to the Right to Information.
solution: False. The Right to Information has reduced secrecy in the working of the government, not increased it. Under the Right to Information Act of 2005 every citizen may apply to the information officer of any government office, department, public undertaking or aided institution and ask for records, files, orders, accounts and reports, and the officer is bound to supply the information within a fixed period, ordinarily thirty days. Only a few matters, such as those affecting the security and sovereignty of the country, are kept out of its reach. Because of this Act the files and decisions of the administration have been opened to the public gaze, the working of the government has become transparent, officers and ministers have become answerable to the people for their acts, and corruption, favouritism and delay have been exposed in many cases. The correct statement is therefore : Secrecy in the working of Government has decreased and transparency has increased due to the Right to Information.

subject: Political Science
context: State whether the following statements are true or false. Give reasons for your answers (any two) :
stem: State whether the following statement is true or false and give the reason for your answer : Coalition politics leads to instability.
solution: True. A coalition government is formed when no single party wins a majority of seats and several parties, often with different ideologies, programmes and regional interests, come together to run the government. Because the partners do not share a common outlook, they quarrel over the distribution of ministries and over policy; the smaller allies bargain, press their own demands and threaten to walk out. If even one important partner withdraws its support the government loses its majority and falls before completing its five-year term, and midterm elections become necessary. Decisions on important national questions get delayed or diluted, because every step needs the consent of all the allies, and the Prime Minister or Chief Minister cannot take a firm line. India saw several such short-lived governments at the Centre between 1977 and 1999. For these reasons coalition politics is said to lead to instability, although it must be added that a coalition of parties with a common minimum programme, such as those that completed full terms after 1999, can also give a stable government and make the administration more representative.

subject: Political Science
context: Explain the following concept (any one) :
stem: Explain the following concept : Provisions for minorities.
solution: A minority is a group which is smaller in number than the rest of the population and which differs from it in religion, language or culture. In India the Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains and Parsis are notified as religious minorities, and there are linguistic minorities in every State. Since a minority may be neglected or dominated by the majority, the Constitution makes special provisions to protect it. Articles 25 to 28 give every person freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practise and propagate religion. Article 29 gives every section of citizens having a distinct language, script or culture of its own the right to conserve it, and forbids denial of admission to a State-aided educational institution on grounds of religion, race, caste or language. Article 30 gives all minorities, whether based on religion or language, the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice, and forbids the State to discriminate against such institutions while granting aid. Article 350A provides for instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage for children of linguistic minority groups. Besides these constitutional rights, a National Commission for Minorities was set up in 1992 to safeguard their interests and enquire into complaints, a Ministry of Minority Affairs was created in 2006, and schemes such as scholarships, hostels, skill-training and the Prime Minister's fifteen-point programme are run for their educational and economic development. These provisions secure equality, protect the identity of minorities and strengthen national unity.

subject: Political Science
context: Explain the following concept (any one) :
stem: Explain the following concept : Workers movements.
solution: A workers' movement is the organised effort of industrial workers and other wage-earners to secure their rights and to improve their conditions of work and life. Such movements began with the growth of factories, where the workers had to labour for very long hours for low wages, in unsafe and unhealthy surroundings, with no leave, no security of employment and no protection against accident. Their demands have been fair and timely wages, an eight-hour working day, weekly rest and paid leave, safe working conditions, bonus, provident fund and gratuity, security of employment, housing and medical facilities, the abolition of child labour, and above all the right to organise into trade unions and the right to strike. The instruments of the movement are the trade union, collective bargaining, petitions, morchas, gheraos, strikes and, on the other side, negotiation and arbitration. In India the workers' movement began in the late nineteenth century; Narayan Meghaji Lokhande, a colleague of Mahatma Phule, organised the Bombay Mill-hands Association in 1884 and is regarded as its father, and the All India Trade Union Congress was founded in 1920. As a result of these movements the government passed protective labour laws such as the Factories Act, the Minimum Wages Act, the Industrial Disputes Act and the Workmen's Compensation Act. Workers' movements have thus won social and economic justice for the working class and have strengthened democracy by organising the weaker sections.

stem:
Complete the following chart. As printed, the top box reads 'The Electoral Process' and it branches into two boxes, 'Role of the Election Commission' and 'Role of the Voters'; under each of these two boxes there are two blank lines numbered (1) and (2):

| The Electoral Process | |
|---|---|
| Role of the Election Commission | Role of the Voters |
| (1) ______ | (1) ______ |
| (2) ______ | (2) ______ |

Write the appropriate answers in the blanks.
solution:
The completed chart is:

| The Electoral Process | |
|---|---|
| Role of the Election Commission | Role of the Voters |
| (1) To conduct free, fair and impartial elections — to announce the programme of the election, fix the constituencies, get the voters' list prepared and revised, accept and scrutinise nominations, allot symbols to parties and candidates, appoint the polling staff and observers, arrange the polling and the counting, and declare the results. | (1) To get one's name entered in the voters' list, obtain the voter identity card, and go to the polling booth and vote in every election without fail. |
| (2) To lay down and enforce the Model Code of Conduct on parties and candidates, to keep watch on election expenditure and on the misuse of government machinery, to grant recognition and reserved symbols to political parties, and to order re-polling or to countermand an election when malpractice occurs. | (2) To vote thoughtfully and fearlessly — to study the candidates and the programmes of the parties and vote on merit and not under the influence of caste, religion, language, money, gifts or threats; to refuse to take part in any malpractice, to report it, and afterwards to keep watch on the work of the representative elected. |

The Election Commission is the constitutional authority which conducts the elections, while the voters are the real masters in a democracy; free and fair elections are possible only when both play their part honestly.

subject: Political Science
context: Do as directed (any one) :
stem: Complete the following concept map. As printed, the central box reads 'Social challenges faced by Indian Democracy' and four empty circles are joined to it by arrows (one above, one below, one on the left and one on the right). Write an appropriate social challenge in each of the four blank circles.
solution:
The four blank circles may be filled as follows:

| Circle | Social challenge | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| Above | Casteism | Thinking and acting only in the interest of one's own caste — in voting, in giving jobs and tickets, and in marriage — which divides society and defeats the ideal of equality. |
| Left | Communalism | Regarding one's own religious community as supreme and other communities as rivals or enemies, which leads to hatred, riots and a threat to national unity and secularism. |
| Right | Regionalism | Extreme attachment to one's own region, state or language and hostility to people of other regions, leading to demands for separate states, water and boundary disputes and 'sons of the soil' agitations. |
| Below | Gender discrimination (inequality of women) | The unequal treatment of women in the family and in society — in education, property, wages, health and participation in politics — together with practices such as female foeticide and dowry. |

Other social challenges that may be written are poverty and illiteracy, untouchability, linguistic conflict, and the problems of the backward and tribal sections. All of them come in the way of the social equality and fraternity promised in the Preamble of the Constitution, and Indian democracy must overcome them by education, awareness, strict enforcement of the law and social reform.

subject: Political Science
context: Answer in brief (any one) :
stem: State the norms that are set by the Election Commission to get recognition as a national party.
solution:
The Election Commission of India registers political parties and grants them recognition as a State party or as a National party. A registered party is recognised as a NATIONAL party if it fulfils any one of the following norms :

(1) It secures at least six per cent of the valid votes polled in a general election to the Lok Sabha or to the Legislative Assembly in four or more States, and in addition wins at least four seats in the Lok Sabha; or

(2) It wins at least two per cent of the total seats in the Lok Sabha (that is, at least eleven seats in the present House of 543), and these members are elected from at least three different States; or

(3) It is recognised as a State party in at least four States.

A party that is recognised as a National party gets a symbol reserved for it all over the country, free time on Akashvani and Doordarshan during elections, copies of the electoral rolls free of cost, a larger number of star campaigners, and space for its offices; its recognition is reviewed by the Commission after every general election.

subject: Political Science
context: Answer in brief (any one) :
stem: Which factors are required for the success of democracy in India ?
solution:
The success of democracy in India depends upon the following factors :

(1) Education and literacy — an educated citizen can judge the parties and the candidates, understand public questions and use the vote wisely.

(2) Political awareness and active participation — citizens must vote in every election, take part in public discussion and in the work of local self-governing bodies, and must not remain indifferent.

(3) Free, fair and regular elections conducted by an independent Election Commission, with the Model Code of Conduct strictly enforced.

(4) Honest, capable and responsible leadership, and political parties that work by democratic methods and place the national interest above party interest.

(5) A strong and constructive opposition which criticises the government, checks its mistakes and offers an alternative.

(6) An independent and impartial judiciary and the rule of law, so that the rights of citizens and the Constitution are protected.

(7) A free press and independent media, which inform the people and expose wrongdoing.

(8) Economic and social equality — the removal of poverty, unemployment, casteism, communalism, regionalism and the inequality of women, because political equality has little meaning without social and economic justice.

(9) Freedom from corruption and from the criminalisation of politics, and transparency in public life through instruments such as the Right to Information.

(10) Decentralisation of power through panchayati raj and municipal bodies, and a spirit of tolerance, secularism and national unity among the people.
